title: Air India's $400 Million Fleet Overhaul Takes Shape as Retrofitted Dreamliners Return to Service
excerpt: The Tata-owned carrier has begun receiving retrofitted Boeing 787-8s with new three-class cabins, while inducting factory-fresh 787-9 Dreamliners as part of its largest fleet modernization since privatization.
body:
• Air India's first retrofitted Boeing 787-8 returned to Delhi in April 2026 after a nose-to-tail cabin overhaul at Boeing's facility in Victorville, California
  • The $400 million retrofit program covers 26 legacy 787-8s and 13 Boeing 777-300ERs, with full completion now expected by 2029
  • Two new factory-built Boeing 787-9 Dreamliners have joined the fleet in 2026, with six total widebody deliveries planned this year
  • By end of 2026, Air India expects over 55% of its widebody fleet to feature modernized cabin interiors

First Retrofitted 787 Enters Service

Air India's long-awaited cabin transformation is becoming tangible. The airline's first retrofitted Boeing 787-8, registered VT-ANT, arrived in Delhi on April 13, 2026, after undergoing a comprehensive upgrade at Boeing's Modification Center in Victorville, California, followed by repainting at an FAA-certified facility in San Bernardino.

The overhaul required 12,825 manhours over 45 days, according to the airline. Workers stripped legacy interiors and installed new seating, Thales AVANT Up inflight entertainment systems, fresh carpeting, wall laminates, and upgraded galleys and lavatories. The exterior repainting alone took a 20-member team 18 days and more than 5,700 manhours.

"The new cabin interiors on this aircraft will soon become the standard across our entire Boeing 787 fleet."

— Campbell Wilson, CEO, Air India

The retrofit converts each 787-8 from a two-class layout to a three-class configuration — business, premium economy, and economy — aligning it with the standards set by Air India's newer 787-9 aircraft.

New Dreamliners Join the Fleet

Alongside the retrofit program, Air India has been inducting factory-fresh widebody aircraft. The carrier took delivery of its first custom-built Boeing 787-9 (VT-AWA) in January 2026 — the first new Dreamliner since privatization. The aircraft entered commercial service in February on the Mumbai-Frankfurt route, featuring 296 seats across three classes with flat-bed business seats, QLED HDR touchscreens, Bluetooth headphone pairing, and wireless charging.

A second made-for-Air India 787-9 (VT-AWB) arrived in Delhi in May 2026 after a non-stop flight from Charleston, South Carolina. The airline plans to induct a total of six new widebody aircraft during 2026, including additional 787-9s and Airbus A350-1000s.

Air India now operates 33 Boeing 787s — 26 legacy 787-8s and seven 787-9s — within a total fleet of around 185 aircraft.

Program Timeline and Delays

The retrofit timeline has shifted. Air India originally targeted mid-2027 to complete the 787-8 upgrades, but a senior airline official said in April 2026 that the broader $400 million program — covering both 787s and 777s — would wrap up by 2029, according to The Hindu BusinessLine. Supply chain disruptions, delayed seat certifications, and pandemic-era manpower shortages have all contributed to the slippage.

Air India expects another seven to eight retrofitted 787-8s to rejoin the fleet by end of 2026, with all 26 completed by March 2028, according to Livemint. The 13 Boeing 777-300ER aircraft are scheduled for completion by late 2028 or 2029.

What NRI Travelers Can Expect

For diaspora travelers who have long endured complaints about broken seats, outdated entertainment systems, and worn cabins on Air India's long-haul flights, the changes are arriving. CEO Campbell Wilson told The Hindu BusinessLine that over 50% of the airline's international services would be operated with upgraded aircraft by end of 2026.

The airline is also investing in ground infrastructure. A new premium international lounge at Delhi Airport opened earlier this year, with upgrades planned at facilities in San Francisco and New York JFK — two of the busiest corridors for Indian-American travelers.

The Bigger Picture

The fleet overhaul is the centerpiece of Vihaan.AI, the five-year transformation plan launched after the Tata Group reacquired Air India from the Indian government in January 2022. The conglomerate placed orders for 470 aircraft — 350 from Airbus and 220 from Boeing — making it one of the largest commercial aviation deals in history.

Wilson has likened the current phase to "the morning of the fifth day" of a Test match — the hard work is done, and the results are close but not fully realized. Whether the airline can deliver on its promises fast enough to reclaim market share from Gulf carriers and IndiGo on international routes remains the central question of this transformation.
